cells.tense: You're reading the room right now and you know it — the details land, nothing here is being forced.
cells.ask: Say one true thing out loud that you'd normally keep as a private read — small, specific, and today.
cells.core:
You can sit with someone and see them clearly without turning them into a project. What you notice doesn't come out as a verdict, and it doesn't come out as a performance either — it waits, accurate, there when they are. That's not common.

There's room here to go outward. You know a true thing about someone near you and you're keeping it in your own head, where it's safe. Say it once — not as advice, not as correction, just as what you see. The risk isn't that you're wrong about them; it's that you've been right and silent. A short sentence, said plainly, at the table you're already at.
cells.sheetLine: You see people clearly and you've been keeping it to yourself.
cells.verb: telling real from almost-real, holding many true things at once without flattening them
cells.place: in the space between you and someone you are trying to meet — where what you know about them and what you feel with them have to stay in the same room

cells.tense: You're already living in how this conversation is going to go — reading ahead, bracing for a version that hasn't happened yet.
cells.ask: Let the next thing you notice stay unnamed for one full minute — no conclusion out loud, no fix, just look and wait.
cells.core:
With someone in front of you, some part of you is managing the next ten minutes: anticipating what they'll say, pre-reading the mood, deciding what it means before they've finished meaning it. You're not making it up — you're picking up something real — but you're running ahead of the person in the room, and you end up talking to your read of them instead of to them.

What that costs is what you're good at: being present to someone as they are, not as you've already filed them. Let the next thing you notice go unnamed. No conclusion spoken, no gentle correction, no summary — a minute of watching and letting them arrive in their own time. If your read was right, it'll still be right in a minute. And the minute itself takes nothing from you.
cells.sheetLine: You're reading people faster than they can arrive.

cells.tense: You keep not-quite-saying what you see, holding back on a read you'd once have trusted without thinking about it.
cells.ask: Ask one friend one real question about their life — not the safe version, the one you actually want to know.
cells.core:
You're sitting with someone and you're half elsewhere. They're telling you something, you're nodding, tracking the shape of it, and the part of you that knows what's true has gone quiet — you don't trust your read enough to say it, and you don't let yourself rest in not knowing either. So you stay on the surface, pleasant, one step back.

Insight isn't what's absent here; contact is. Ask one person one real question — something you actually want to know about their life, not the version that keeps the conversation safe. You're not fixing anything, just stepping into the room you're already standing in. Curious is enough to start.

cells.tense: You're already steering how people see themselves — a word here, a look there — and calling it just paying attention.
cells.ask: Name one thing you said to someone recently that you'd call fairness if you were asked — say it to yourself, plainly, and own it.
cells.core:
You can feel when a conversation is tipping before anyone's asked. Your read of the room shapes what you say — a small correction, a redirect, a tone — and it lands. That's discernment doing real work, in real time, through how you treat people.

You'd describe it as just being decent, or just being clear, and it doesn't feel like a decision you made. But you're shaping what people come away believing about each other and themselves. Pick one thing you said recently — one moment where you were fair to someone — and call it what it was. The work is already yours; naming it just means you know where it comes from.
cells.sheetLine: You're already shaping how people see right and wrong. You're calling it just being fair.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim I had to cut was telling the person what they were holding back and why; the record only gives me the capacity and its motion, so the Too Little cell locates the quiet without naming a cause or a room. A reader might reasonably say the seat still feels a little abstract — compassion is not a feeling to describe but a way of being with someone — so I brought it down to an actual conversation, a friend, a table. The ask survives being wrong in every cell because it is a size anyone can try once, and if the reading is off the experiment still returns something; the sentence that served me more than them was an early line about 'wearing truths lightly' and it is gone.
